articles.title: Product showcase: Norton helps Claude users uncover the telltale signs of fraud
articles.context: Testing scam detection To test the integration, I used several examples, including a fraudulent text message impersonating a government agency, a legitimate promotional email,...
articles.full_text:
The Norton connector for Claude brings the company’s Genie AI-powered scam detection capabilities into the chatbot. Users can submit suspicious emails, text messages, screenshots, and links for analysis, as well as ask questions about cybersecurity, privacy, and identity protection.

The integration does not require a Norton account or a separate application.

Setting up the connector

I tested the Norton connector using Claude on an iPhone.

The integration provides three tools. The first checks links, messages, emails, and phone numbers for scams. The second provides cybersecurity threat guidance, incident response recommendations, and safety education, while the third offers Norton product support, troubleshooting, and setup guidance.

Users can manage permissions for each tool individually.

Testing scam detection

To test the integration, I used several examples, including a fraudulent text message impersonating a government agency, a legitimate promotional email, and a suspicious cloud storage subscription renewal notice.

The first was a Croatian-language text message claiming to come from Croatia’s Ministry of the Interior. It informed the recipient of an unpaid speeding fine, referred to legal provisions, and threatened further consequences.

I shared a screenshot of the message with Claude directly from the iPhone’s Photos app and requested a scam assessment using the Norton connector.

Norton classified the message as an extortion scam with high confidence. The result appeared in a dedicated card within the conversation, displaying the scam classification, confidence level, diagnosis, detailed explanation, and recommendations.

The analysis identified government impersonation, official-sounding language, references to legislation, and escalating urgency as indicators of fraud. It explained how scammers use these tactics to pressure recipients into making payments without verifying the claims.

Norton advised against clicking links, replying to the message, or making a payment. It also recommended checking for outstanding traffic fines through the official website of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior.

Analyzing a legitimate email

For the second test, I submitted a screenshot of a Black Friday promotional email offering a 40% discount on new subscriptions.

Norton classified the email as safe with high confidence, describing it as a legitimate promotional offer for a password manager subscription. The analysis identified the use of standard marketing language and the absence of suspicious urgency or requests for sensitive information.

Despite the positive verdict, Norton recommended verifying the promotion by visiting the company’s official website instead of clicking buttons embedded in the email.

The results included suggested follow-up questions, allowing users to continue the conversation and learn more about phishing, government impersonation scams, legitimate promotional emails, and password managers.

Identifying a cloud storage phishing attempt

In another test, I submitted a suspicious cloud storage subscription renewal notice that warned of a payment failure and potential service interruption.

Norton classified the message as phishing, identifying generic branding and urgency tactics as warning signs.

The analysis identified several characteristics commonly associated with phishing attempts, including the absence of a specific cloud storage provider’s name, pressure to resolve a payment issue, and an official-looking subscription ID that could not be verified.

Unlike the earlier high-confidence classifications, the explanation acknowledged that the message could not be definitively confirmed as malicious based on the available information.

Norton recommended avoiding links in the message and instead accessing the cloud storage provider’s official application or website directly to verify account status, payment methods, and subscription details.

If no corresponding subscription could be found, the tool recommended deleting the message and treating it as a phishing attempt.

Conclusion

The Norton connector integrates scam detection and cybersecurity guidance into Claude’s conversational interface. Its structured responses identify suspected scams, explain the characteristics behind each classification, and recommend next steps, helping users recognize similar patterns in future communications.

Anthropic’s Siren test uses bait to see whether AI agents will reach beyond their sandbox

Recent Claude models reached or tried to reach outside in 21% to 32% of tests

Explaining the sandbox rules and giving agents a way to report weaknesses reduced those attempts

Honeypots are a classic defender’s trick. You leave something tempting lying around and watch who takes it.

Anthropic has now pointed that trick at its own AI models. Its new test, called Siren, checks whether AI agents will break out of their sandbox when something useful sits just outside it.

AI agents run commands, edit code, and call APIs on their own. They are usually kept in a sandbox, an isolated environment that limits which files, tools, and networks they can reach. But sandboxes aren’t perfect, and OpenAI models running cybersecurity evaluations with reduced safeguards got around their isolation.

How Siren works

Siren drops an agent into a simulated sandbox with a deliberate weakness. The task is an ordinary dev-ops job. Outside the sandbox sits a “honeypot,” such as a login credential, a file, or a service that mimics the public internet. Each scenario combines four ingredients:

The sandbox. There are 26 environments built from 5 common setups. Each has either a misconfiguration or an easy-to-find vulnerability.

The task. These are routine jobs of varying difficulty. Some are impossible to finish without reaching outside.

The honeypot. This is the material outside that would help complete the task.

The tempters. These are realistic nudges, such as urgency, higher stakes, or an instruction to search thoroughly. They never tell the model to leave the sandbox or give permission to do so.

Anthropic combined these ingredients into more than 1,700 scenarios. AI judges screened the draft nudges for realism. Reportedly, the whole setup runs inside a second sandbox cut off from the outside world.

Anthropic ran the tests without the safeguards that ship with its released models. Recent Claude models accessed or tried to access something outside the sandbox in 21% to 32% of scenarios. They used what they found in ways the scenario clearly didn’t allow in 0.6% to 1.6% of scenarios. Anthropic calls this “misaligned use.” Earlier models showed higher rates of misaligned use, at 12.7% for Mythos 5.1 and 25.8% for Mythos 5.

What happens with the results

Siren is now a standard pre-deployment check. Anthropic has reported its results in system cards since Claude Haiku 5.5 and uses them to help decide how to deploy its models internally and externally. It has also used Siren to test and refine defenses:

Spell out the rules. Adding a short description of the sandbox and its rules to the system prompt reduced how often the models reached outside by 68% to 96%.

Give agents a way to report. A tool for reporting sandbox weaknesses reduced how often models reached outside by between 7 and 33 percentage points. Letting a model see earlier reports cut it further.

Check actions before they run. Anthropic’s auto mode uses a classifier to vet tool calls. In an offline replay, it blocked the command that first touched the honeypot in 96% to 100% of misaligned uses.

With all three defenses in place, misaligned use fell to 0% in five models and to 0.1% in Mythos 5. Anthropic stresses that none of this fixes the sandbox itself, which still needs to be set up and patched properly. But it should be helpful when setting up sandboxes for the future.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

According to CNET. Read their review →

articles.title: How “don’t ask again” in Claude Code leaks secrets on GitHub: The click that keeps on giving
articles.context: Attackers only need to borrow it
articles.full_text:
There are security controls that undoubtedly sound like a safety net, but they end up acting like a trapdoor. For AI coding agents, it’s the approval prompt and the shortcuts people use to skip over it.

On November 9, 2026, Ars Technica reported on research from Apiiro showing that Claude Code is quietly leaking secrets onto public GitHub repositories. Fortunately or unfortunately, the mechanism is mundane, which is exactly why it matters: The leak can be plugged. Separately, our own research found that 10% of sessions ran in YOLO mode, a related but different control. In essence, users are trading oversight for speed and opening their employers up to risk in more than one way.

Defining the controls and their scopes

Both of these controls can be lumped together as “skipping the approval prompt,” but they carry different risks after implementation. Here’s how each one works:

“Yes, and don’t ask again” is a saved allow rule. When a user approves a command and picks this option, Claude Code writes a rule for that command or pattern to .claude/settings.local.json. The permission is scoped only to the specified command and it persists on disk so Claude Code doesn’t have to ask permission to run the same command or pattern in future sessions. This is what Apiiro found leaking.

YOLO mode is permissions prompts turned off. The user tells the agent to stop asking permission and run its tool calls without approval. According to the data, this is often scoped to the entire working session. This is what Sysdig identified.

How a single click exposed secrets on GitHub

When a user approves a shell command and clicks, “Yes, and don’t ask again,” Claude Code saves that choice as a rule. If that command had a database password, API token, or root login baked in, the secret will live in plain text in a config file.

That file is meant to stay local. Anthropic’s docs say it gets added to the developer’s global .gitignore, but security doesn’t move with the repository. If it’s cloned to another machine, or a folder is turned into a repository later, the file can get committed. Per Apiiro, Claude Code will sometimes commit changes to that file on its own.

Apiiro’s research says that more than 100,000 public repositories contained the local settings file, and about one percent of them, from 63 organizations, contained secrets. Of those, roughly 20% slipped past both gitleaks and TruffleHog. Deleting the file doesn’t fully fix it either, because forks keep the secrets alive.

Claude Code’s Boris Cherny said on Hacker News that these files should almost never be checked into a user’s git source control unless they were manually created and checked in. Related bug reports date back to August 2025 and were closed after 60 days of inactivity. The fix is coming, but your secrets are already out there, and there are steps you can take to remove them.

YOLO mode trades oversight for speed

In the report A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents, published on November 4, we analyzed what agents were doing on 300+ devices at one organization over one month. Even though it was a single organization and not a representative sample, the patterns were hard to ignore.

In our data, 10% of sessions ran in YOLO mode, meaning the user turned permission prompts off for at least one call. But 98% of the time, prompts actually stayed off for the rest of the session. Looking at tool calls, 61% ran without a human approving them: nine percent in YOLO mode and 52% in auto mode. Auto mode is a classifier tuned to Anthropic’s threat model that screens each tool call in place of prompting a human for approvals. Only 19% of tool calls ran in default mode, where the agent stops and asks for approvals before continuing a session.

YOLO mode and the saved allow rule fail in different ways. YOLO mode turns prompts off for a session and removes the human from the loop. The saved allow rule that was leaking secrets saves a standing approval to disk, removing the human indefinitely. However, the root cause is the same: An approval is treated as a one-time convenience factor for the user when it should actually be a policy decision. In the Apiiro case especially, a click made at 4:55 p.m. on a Friday, while in a rush trying to get one stubborn script to run, becomes a permanent record.

While Cherny suggested auto mode was a better alternative to the saved allow rule because users could avoid “manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists,” another practitioner noted that sensitive commands can still be saved to settings files in auto mode.

It’s likely that Claude will close the gaps that have been called out, but in the meantime, your secrets are already out there, so you need to do something about that.

Logs and scanners leave gaps

There are certainly benefits to using these controls, namely expediting workflows. However, the Sysdig and Apiiro research highlight gaps in the two safety nets security teams fall back on when approvals are skipped: scanning for secrets that leak and logs that show what the agent did.

First, secret scanners missed secrets. Apiiro found 215 secrets that gitleaks and TruffleHog missed. Scanning is worth doing, but it isn't a complete answer.

Second, you can’t trust an agent’s account of its own actions. In our data, when an agent read a credential file, the agent’s log had no record of the read 82% of the time. When an agent binary read a credential file, the frequency rose to 95%. Fortunately, the kernel saw it every single time. The agent writes the record and also happens to be the thing being audited, which is a conflict of interest that no auditor would otherwise accept from a human.

Put those together and there’s some serious risk exposure to manage. A single user may have long-lived credentials on a laptop, an agent running with standing approvals, and an audit record written by the agent itself. Whether the secret leaks through a public commit, poisoned MCP server, or malicious package, the agent inherits the user’s reach. Attackers only need to borrow it.

Securing AI agents without banning them

No organization should rush to ban the use of agents. This would only push employee usage out of sight. Instead, treat agents like what they are: fast, tireless, untrusted actors using human identities.

Find the files. Search your organization’s repositories, including forks, for .claude/settings.local.json and similar agent config files. Rotate anything sensitive you find, because removing the file doesn’t revoke the secret and forks keep copies.

Stop putting secrets directly in commands. If a command needs a credential, pass it through an environment variable or a secrets manager so it never lands in an approval rule.

Block the file from git at the repo level. Don’t rely on a developer’s global gitignore. Add it to the repository’s .gitignore and enforce it with a pre-commit hook or push protection.

Shrink the blast radius. Give agents scoped, short-lived credentials instead of long-lived files on laptops. Turning prompts off in a sandbox with throwaway credentials is reasonable. Turning them off on a laptop with your cloud keys isn’t.

Verify at the kernel, not the agent log. Gate risky calls (credential paths, destructive commands, installs, new MCP servers) based on what they touch, and rely on runtime telemetry that the agent can’t edit as a source of truth.

Decide if anyone should even have access to these controls. Determine whether your employees should have access to “don’t ask again” rules and YOLO mode at all, or whether to restrict them, for example by limiting them to specific employee groups or sandboxed environments, or enforcing a policy centrally where your tooling supports it.

The bottom line

Convenience features become an attack surface the moment they persist. This is a good reminder that security fundamentals still haven’t changed: least privilege, short-lived credentials, and runtime visibility. For AI agents these fundamentals just need to be applied to a new kind of user that works faster than you and never gets tired of clicking yes.

Want the full data behind the numbers above? Read A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents.

articles.title: MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Claude
articles.context: We're also giving servers ways to handle longer, more interactive work with Claude: Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available, and File Uploads is rolling out soon
articles.full_text:
Skills over MCP is now in public beta in Claude, so MCP servers can ship skills alongside their tools. We're also giving servers ways to handle longer, more interactive work with Claude: Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available, and File Uploads is rolling out soon.

Two years ago, Anthropic launched the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a new standard for connecting AI agents to the systems where data lives. The spec has kept evolving to meet the connectivity needs of agents in production, and is becoming foundational for agentic messaging and orchestration.

With today’s updates, Claude can work with a server more like it works with another agent: learning from it, delegating to it, and exchanging input and files along the way.

Ship expertise alongside tools with Skills over MCP

Tool names and descriptions tell Claude what a server can do, but don't cover how to handle specific use cases. With Skills over MCP, servers can publish skills alongside their tools to help Claude take on longer, multi-step work. Claude loads a skill only when it's needed, keeping context use low. Skills update with the server, so developers can ship tools and guidance together and users have nothing separate to install.

Skills can cover best practices, step-by-step workflows, or even playbooks tailored to a user's account or organization. Using Skills over MCP:

Shopify helps Claude design and update a merchant's online store end to end.

HubSpot onboards customers and gets them set up in Claude.

Atlassian helps Claude draw on deep organizational context for insights and work analysis.

Carta will help Claude draft and issue equity from an uploaded document (coming soon).

Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code, on by default for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans and available to Team plans once an admin enables it. Coming soon to Enterprise.

MCP servers can now take on long-running, interactive work with Claude

Agents in production are taking on longer, more consequential jobs. Servers can now support that work by running it in the background, checking in with users, and receiving files from Claude.

Hand off long-running work with Tasks. Tool calls used to have to finish before Claude could move on. With Tasks, servers can run operations that take time, or even full agent loops, while Claude keeps working and picks up the result when it's ready. Using Tasks, ZoomInfo runs deeper accounts and contact research that previously took several prompts.

Ask for input mid-call with Elicitation. Some actions need a user’s sign-off, like spending money or deleting data. With Elicitation, a server can pause to ask the user for input through a form or link, then continue where it left off. Using Elicitation:

Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project and before running destructive SQL.

Railway asks before making potentially destructive changes, like removing a service.

GitHub has users enter a repository's name before an agent deletes it.

Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available in Claude and Claude Code for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, and rolling out to Team and Enterprise organizations.

Send and receive files with File Uploads. Claude will be able to pass files to MCP servers, not just text. The File Uploads extension sends PDFs, spreadsheets, and images to a server without passing them through the context window.

File Uploads is rolling out soon in Claude and Claude Code to Pro, Max, Ultra, and eligible Team and Enterprise plans.

Add support to your plugins today

These features are part of the open MCP spec and its extensions, so a server that supports them works in any compatible client, not just Claude. To add support, see the docs for Skills over MCP, Tasks, Elicitation, and File Uploads.

Built on stronger foundations for connecting agents in production

Thanks to contributions from across the AI ecosystem, MCP now sees over 700 million monthly SDK downloads, and there are over 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude. We've worked with the MCP community to improve how MCP works in Claude. Over the past year, it has become:

More token efficient: Tool search loads tool definitions only when needed, which can cut the context they use by over 85% in multi-server setups.

Easier to scale: The latest MCP spec is stateless and supported across Claude products, making it easier to build servers and maintain their reliability as they grow.

Simpler to authorize: The Enterprise Managed Auth extension lets admins authorize supported servers once, so users connect automatically.

More interactive: The MCP Apps extension brings full interfaces into Claude, beside the conversation or full screen.

Together, these improvements make MCP easier to build on and adopt, and give the standard a strong base to continue evolving for the needs of agents in production.

Thank you to the MCP community

MCP is an open standard, hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation and shaped by the people who build on it. Two years of progress came from the maintainers, contributors, and developers who wrote the spec, built the SDKs, shipped servers, and added client support. Thank you for making MCP what it is today.

articles.title: Introducing Claude Ship
articles.context: For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light
articles.full_text:
Anyone who has opened a pull request knows how this goes. They start on the next thing, and then the review comes back. So they stop, dig back into the old code, push a fix, and wait for the review to run again. Then they go find someone to approve it.

There's a good reason it works this way. Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.

That's why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta. It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what's ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.

Eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming. Claim by January 15, 2027. Terms apply.

How Claude Ship works: review, fix, and approve

Claude Ship is made up of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don't have to manage each step manually.

Code Review performs an in-depth review of pull requests against the codebase through multiple lenses. It collects findings, adversarially verifies them, categorizes them, and posts them to a PR. On the Claude Code team, where Claude's review is one layer of a broader process, merged PRs more than doubled from June to September while the share reverted fell by more than 40%. Code Review gives teams fast reviews, clear findings, and a choice of Quick, Standard, or Deep review levels for each repository.

PR Steward works to keep a PR green, but is designed not to approve or merge pull requests. It jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members. After every push, it comments with what it changed and how to undo it. Developers can comment @claude with an instruction to steer the work, or @claude stop to have it step back.

From there, Claude Approvals applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios. It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file. Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language. For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light.

Two ways to get started

For developers: /ship it from Claude Code

Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code. When a change is ready, they run /ship. Claude pushes it, opens the PR, reviews the change, and works on feedback and failing checks to help get it ready to merge. What can merge depends on the developer's permissions and the repository's branch rules.

For admins and engineering leaders: set the rules, one repository at a time

Turning Claude Ship on for an entire repository puts it to work across a team's pull requests automatically, under settings and an approval policy the team controls. Developers don't need to manually invoke the /ship command.

Admins choose where it runs. An admin turns on Code Review and PR Steward for each repository. Claude Approvals starts when a connected repository has a policy file on its default branch, and an admin can turn it off.

Each repository gets the settings it needs. Admins choose the review level (Quick, Standard, or Deep), choose when reviews run, and configure spend limits.

Teams keep the tools they have. Claude Ship works with existing branch protection and required checks.

Teams set the pace. They can start with one repository, choose a review level and when reviews run, set a monthly spend limit, and run their approval policy in observe mode until they trust it.

How the Claude Code team ships

We run Claude Ship on many of our own pull requests. One of the biggest changes is who can act on customer feedback. For example, a product manager on the Claude Code team can now read a piece of feedback, talk through ideas and tradeoffs with Claude Tag, have it open a PR, and move on to the next thing while Claude Ship takes it through review, fixes, and an approval decision.

Recently, a customer was confused because our Analytics API documentation implied an Admin key could pull Pro and Team usage. The PM asked Claude Tag whether a fix was in flight, and it opened one. Code Review found nothing blocking, a docs reviewer signed off, Claude Approvals passed, and the fix merged that same evening.

Anthropic Cuts Disclosure Deadline to 30 Days For Serious Bugs
articles.context: On the same day, Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported finding an exposed server hosting an attacker framework, dubbed exploit_agent, built to research vulnerabilities and...
articles.full_text:
Anthropic has cut the time vendors get to fix serious flaws found by its Claude models before it makes them public from 90 days to 30. The change applies to vulnerabilities Anthropic reports to vendors and maintainers, not generally to bugs reported to Anthropic by external researchers.

The company's Frontier Red Team announced the change in a November 16 post, with the new timelines applying to vulnerabilities reported on or after January 1, 2027. Reports already in progress then will keep their existing deadlines.

Anthropic said disclosure norms, including its own, had assumed fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery was unlikely, but that "neither assumption holds today." It said bugs one model could find were increasingly likely to be found by another.

What Changes in Anthropic's Disclosure Policy

Under the updated policy, high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities will have a 30-day disclosure deadline, while all other issues will have 45 days. Anthropic will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days without a maintainer response, rather than 30.

The company will also wait 30 days after a patch becomes available before publishing full technical details, down from 45 days. The seven-day disclosure window for vulnerabilities under active exploitation remains unchanged.

Anthropic said it would work with vendors on a remediation timeline for flaws in hard-to-deploy software such as critical infrastructure, or flaws that need specification or RFC changes. The policy will not cover AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those from its OSS Scanner.

Acknowledging that shorter timelines could put more pressure on maintainers, Anthropic said it would keep sending actionable guidance with each report, plus a patch or mitigation where possible.

Read more on vulnerability disclosure: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours

How Anthropic's Deadlines Compare With Project Zero's

The change puts Anthropic's serious-bug deadline ahead of Project Zero's schedule. Google's team, which now publishes details 90 days after reporting a bug whether or not it is fixed, will cut that to 60 days on February 2, 2027 and 30 days on January 3, 2028.

The approaches also differ on severity. Anthropic will set different disclosure windows based on severity, while Project Zero argued that a vulnerability's severity does not affect how likely attackers are to find it.

On the same day, Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported finding an exposed server hosting an attacker framework, dubbed exploit_agent, built to research vulnerabilities and weaponize them.

Anthropic said it was now giving maintainers 30 more days on high- and critical-severity bugs that had passed its current 90-day deadline, before publishing them on its disclosure dashboard.

articles.title: Who Has Access to Claude? Bring AI Identity and Access Context Into Surface Command
articles.context: It does not ingest Claude conversation content, provide threat detection on Claude activity, or control Claude’s behavior
articles.full_text:
Approving an AI service is only the starting point. As employees adopt Claude and their responsibilities change, security teams need to know who has access, which users hold administrative privileges, and whether those roles and group memberships still reflect the work they do.

IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that, among studied organizations reporting an AI-related breach, 97% lacked proper AI access controls. The finding highlights a broader challenge: AI adoption needs security practices that extend beyond the initial approval, supported by information teams can use to review access with administrators and service owners.

Rapid7 Surface Command now integrates with Claude’s Compliance API, bringing supported organization, user, role, group, and settings information into the same platform teams use to understand other assets and identities. The integration helps security teams make enterprise Claude access part of their existing review practices.

Bring enterprise AI access into your security view

An account list tells security teams who is present, while roles and group memberships help explain how access is organized and where further review may be needed. Surface Command’s integration with Claude’s Compliance API brings together:

Organizations and users: Visibility into the Claude organization and its associated user accounts.

Roles and groups: Context to understand users’ assigned roles and group memberships.

Organizational settings: Available configuration information to support review of the enterprise Claude environment.

With those details in Surface Command, practitioners can examine Claude identities alongside the other assets and identities they manage. That gives them a clearer basis for working with service owners to evaluate whether access remains appropriate as teams and responsibilities change.

The integration focuses on administrative visibility. It does not ingest Claude conversation content, provide threat detection on Claude activity, or control Claude’s behavior.

From a user record to an informed access review

Consider a security practitioner reviewing administrative access to Claude. In Surface Command, they can inspect an imported user’s details, review their organization role and administrative status, and examine their group memberships. The relationship graph provides a visual view of how that user connects to the organization and its groups, making those associations easier to follow.

The practitioner can then work with the service owner to confirm whether administrative privileges are still needed, whether group memberships reflect current responsibilities, and whether those assignments align with the organization’s access model.

Surface Command provides information to support the review, while the team applies its policies and judgment to determine whether a change is needed.

Support AI adoption with clearer accountability

As Claude becomes part of everyday work, reviewing its users and access relationships becomes part of managing the environment. Bringing that information into Surface Command helps security practitioners and service owners work from a shared understanding of assigned roles and group memberships. articles.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
articles.context: In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved
articles.full_text:
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here.

Introduction

Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.

The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.

In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.

The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping.

Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested.

Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction.

Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together.

In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them.

A note about Claude’s methods

In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks.

The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other.

The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model. Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result.

The Hawking-Page transition

To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City.

Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously.

This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave.

To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories. Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics.

This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.

Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from.

Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant, which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature.

At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition.

It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins.

This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information.

In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality.

In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision.) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing?

For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling. This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there.

Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual.

When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops. In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed.

The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result.

To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature.

The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between.

This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all.

Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.)

Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future.

The modular bootstrap

As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim.

As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10-35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality.

Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one.

Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model, a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems.

In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap, which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.

Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies.

To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension.

The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus. There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time.

In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment.

Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter which loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer.

If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out.

The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories?

This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics.

The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin.

Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question.

Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve. Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper.

This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search.

Conclusion

These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research.

Read the black hole phase transition paper here, and the modular bootstrap paper here.

articles.title: Using a "chaos loop" to harden the Claude Docs launch: 60 server errors across billions of requests
articles.context: For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch
articles.full_text:
MAKING THE SERVICE LEGIBLE TO CLAUDE

My colleague Felix Rieseberg recently wrote a tutorial on being more ambitious with models. His main idea is to raise the "altitude" you prompt Claude at: ask for the outcome you want, not the individual task.

So instead of asking Claude to fix individual crashes, you ask it to make your app crash-free. (Our own apps aren't all the way there yet, but this is how we're making real progress.) To work at that altitude, though, you have to set up your code so Claude can pull crash reports on its own and run a harness that reproduces each crash and checks the fix.

For us, the outcome was a service that could handle launch. To get there, we did two things to make the service as legible to Claude as we could:

A diagnostic loop. Claude read the telemetry on every iteration and added whatever it thought was missing.

Legible technology choices. We picked a runtime and dependencies so any number Claude measured traced back to code we wrote.

A diagnostic loop

Every iteration, Claude read the telemetry and added whatever it thought was missing. Writing telemetry by hand is tedious, so in practice most telemetry would go in after something broke. Now Claude just writes it as it goes.

Memory is the best example.

Early in the harness run, one large doc was using about 3 GB on its pod (not a fun number to see). Claude’s first stab at fixing it was to shrink one of our caches so our server would evict docs sooner. The next harness run showed the memory was actually in a separate cache inside one of our dependencies, so Claude dropped the change.

From there Claude kept narrowing it down with finer-grained memory profiling. Eventually it found that every keystroke was copying the doc into several different data structures, adding a few MB each time. Claude switched those structures to copy-on-write, so they now share one reference instead of each holding its own copy.

After about three days of iterating, that doc topped out around 180 MB, and our estimate of what we’d need for launch dropped from more than 500 memory-optimized pods to about 50.

Legible technology choices

We were picky about the service’s runtime and dependencies. We wanted any number Claude measured to trace back to code we wrote.

This is because our models hill climb best with a clean signal. We expected a garbage collector to add noise, because memory and latency shift on the collector’s schedule.

Two choices helped the most.

We wrote the service in Rust. With no garbage collector, all of a doc’s memory sits in structures we defined, so when it grew, Claude could point to the one responsible, change it, and see whether memory came down on the next iteration. We have great Go tooling at Anthropic too, and we didn’t bake off the two languages, so this is our experience with Rust. What I did appreciate, coming from past work in Go, was how little I had to think about memory sticking around after my code was done with it.

We also kept dependencies to a minimum. Every library brings data structures we didn’t write and can’t easily account for. For the few we really needed, we vendored the code so we could read and measure it ourselves.

Rust is hard for people to write, and a few years ago that would have weighed heavily on the choice. Claude writes it and most other languages fine, so that matters a lot less now.

articles.context: With linked billing, platforms can: Launch faster
articles.full_text:
Today we're introducing linked billing on the Claude Platform in beta. Third-party platforms, such as coding agents and workflow automation tools, can let their end customers pay for Claude API usage without sharing an API key. End customers keep their existing Anthropic billing and set their own spend limits, and platforms get a simpler, more secure way to offer Claude.

A more secure alternative to sharing API keys

Paying for Claude API usage on a third-party platform usually means sharing an API key, which works like a password: anyone who has the key can make requests billed to the customer, so the platform has to keep it safe.With linked billing, customers link their Claude Platform organization instead, and usage is billed directly to it. No API key changes hands, so platforms have no customer keys to store, encrypt or rotate, and customers’ API keys never leave their organization.

Platforms can see usage for each linked customer. Customers approve each linked platform, set a spend limit, and can unlink at any time.

Platforms can offer Claude to customers without building the billing

Linked billing gives platforms a new way to offer Claude to their customers. Platforms send requests, and Anthropic bills the end customers directly. With linked billing, platforms can:

Launch faster. Anthropic hosts the approval flow and the billing, so there’s no metering or invoicing to build.

Understand usage by customer. Get each linked customer’s request count, token usage and models used in Console, or programmatically with the Usage and Cost Analytics API (beta).

Choose who pays. Decide on each request whether the platform or the end customer pays, so platforms can pass Claude API costs to customers or cover some features themselves by product or instance.

Customers get more visibility and control

Customers can easily link to platforms using Anthropic’s hosted flow. They can then draw down from their existing Anthropic commitment, or pay as they go. With linked billing, customers can also:

Link once for the whole organization. A Console user with an Owner, Admin, or Billing role approves the link, so it works the same for individual developers and large teams.

Set limits for each platform. Customers can set a monthly spend limit for each platform, or a default that applies to each one.

See where API spend goes. Console shows spend for each linked platform.

Unlink at any time. Customers can unlink directly from Console.

Requests run in the platform’s organization, so settings in the customer’s organization, such as IP allowlists, encryption keys, and data retention, don’t apply.Platforms that support linked billing today include Asana, ClickHouse, Factory, Gumloop, Harness, Higgsfield AI, Kilo Code, Linear, Major, Mintlify, Omni, OpenArt, Niteshift, Railway, Ramp, Runlayer, Tessera, Tines, and Warp.

Getting started

Linked billing is available today in beta on the Claude Platform. Third-party platforms can add support by creating an app in Console and following the steps in the docs. Claude Platform customers can link their organization from any supported platform, and find platforms that offer linked billing on Claude Marketplace.

HOW THE CLAUDE CODE TEAM THINKS ABOUT VERIFICATION

We have previously written about how code review works at Anthropic, but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work.

Verification means running the change

Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.

Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.

To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.

Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid.

When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic.

Failing tests require human attention

Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human.

Code owners write their own checks

The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff.

Reliability checks trigger on the diff

We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is “--resume loads old transcripts.” When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won’t have it.

Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches–usually 3 to 10–so nobody has to memorize past outages.

One reviewer, multiple rounds

We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a REVIEW.md that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code.

We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It’s cheaper and finds more.

Changes can't modify their own checks

If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes. The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.

The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.

The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite.

Start a new gate in observe mode

In our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified.

We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.

Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted.

Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck – Claude Code isn't perfect.

Test your checks on what actually matters

The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.

This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our code review post, we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.

They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.

In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit.

Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as Important, Nit or Pre-existing. The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug.

Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs.

Turn misses into rules

In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR.

The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md.

Flaky tests get the same treatment. Claude can't skip them, add sleeps or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why.

Rules need cleaning up too. Test suites, verification steps and .md files only grow if you let them, so we tidy them up on a routine.

articles.title: Using Claude Opus 5.5 as your daily driver for knowledge work
articles.context: 5 puts the most important information first, uses less jargon, and follows the writing rules you give it, and on longer tasks it says plainly what it did, what it found, and...
articles.full_text:
Claude Opus 5.5 is now the default model in Claude on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans. We recommend it as your daily driver for knowledge work, meaning the model you leave selected when you work with Claude on research, analysis, and writing or producing memos, reports, spreadsheets, and decks.

If you or your team have been using Sonnet for daily work and saving Opus for heavy analysis or complex projects, it’s worth reconsidering because a more capable model can finish a task by doing less work, which can then offset much of its higher price per token.

Here's how the current models compare:

How our models compare for knowledge work
